result:
Review complete — 23 findings reported, ranked most-severe first.

**How it ran:** eight finder agents swept the branch from different angles (line-by-line, removed-behavior, cross-file tracing, altitude, conventions, reuse, simplification, efficiency), I deduplicated their candidates, and five adversarial verifiers checked the consequential single-source claims — two with executable tests against the real code and one with actual production builds.

**The shape of the results:** the flag-OFF path (what end users run today) is clean — the moved debounce adapter was verified byte-identical to the old one, and lint plus all 324 tests pass. Nearly everything serious lives on the corpus-flag-ON path: the worst is the v2-migration guard still probing localStorage so it clobbers OPFS state on every reload, followed by the "dev-only" flag guard existing only in comments (it works in production, where enabling it makes a user's workspace appear wiped), typed corpus errors dead-ending as unhandled rejections or a silent `if (error) return;`, unordered concurrent OPFS writes, a confirmed quota-error-masking bug in `writeFile`'s `finally`, a hydration race that can discard input typed before the async read resolves, and the lost 300ms write debounce. The manifest codec's silent-drop/version-check gaps and the title-slug collision are confirmed real but latent — that code has no production callers until S4. The remainder are reuse/dead-code/docs cleanups.

**One claim was refuted:** two finders believed `process.env?.NEXT_PUBLIC_CORPUS_FS` defeats Next.js env inlining; an empirical Turbopack build showed the optional-chained form is inlined fine (though the static form would be more portable across bundlers) — and that refutation confirmed the env var also enables the flag in production, reinforcing the missing dev-only gate.
